history.title: Feel the Invisible

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Hold two magnets close and you can feel something pushing back through empty air. Nothing is touching. That push is a magnetic **force**, described using a field, and fields are one of the strangest true things in physics.

1. Read **The Push You Can Feel Through Nothing**.
2. Learn the terms in the **Glossary**, then win the **Matching** game and the **Word Scramble**.
3. Keep the **Magnet Rules** chart open while you experiment.
4. Sort the materials in **Will It Stick?** — three of these surprise people.
5. Practise explaining with **Magnet Frames**, then check yourself against the rubric.
6. Take the quiz. Question 4 is the one almost everyone gets wrong.
7. If your class has the **Magnetism Lab** in the STEM Lab, run the Field Walk challenge and find the hidden magnet.
8. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Rules of the Invisible** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
9. Finish with **Design Challenge: A Sorter That Lets Go** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.

One rule for this lesson: every time you predict, say it OUT LOUD before you test. Being wrong out loud is how physics gets learned. 🧲

Picture panels: Facing poles and forces; Two poles and a field; A controlled coil; A compass and Earth’s core. All artwork is text-free. Native captions define the model: coral denotes north, teal denotes south in magnet and compass diagrams. Colors do not identify real materials or polarity. Object identity and alloy are supplied by the card text, not established by appearance. The coin is a deliberately plain silhouette, not a reproduction of a minted design. Sorting predicts sticking to an ordinary stationary classroom magnet; weak magnetic responses and moving-field effects are outside that activity. Force arrows differ from field-direction arrows as each caption explains. Core rings and field curves are schematic. The split-magnet image is a thought experiment, not an instruction to break magnets. Circuit pictures explain switching and are not build plans; use only the teacher-approved current-limited classroom kit or a non-electrical model. A core can retain magnetism after current stops. Educator review is pending.

history.title: The Push You Can Feel Through Nothing
history.data:
## The Push You Can Feel Through Nothing

Hold two bar magnets near one another. You can feel a push or pull before they touch. That is a force acting across a gap.

A simple bar magnet has north and south **poles**. With the magnets held aligned, opposite facing poles **attract** and like facing poles **repel**. A freely turning magnet can rotate, changing which poles face each other.

Imagine dividing a bar magnet across its middle. Each piece becomes a smaller magnet with both poles; this does not isolate a north-only or south-only magnet. Treat this as a thought experiment, not a cutting activity.

A **magnetic field** describes magnetic influence at each location. Field lines are a model of direction and relative strength, not physical threads. Iron filings can reveal a pattern because they become magnetized and align with the local field. Use a sealed field viewer for a classroom observation. Outside a bar magnet, field direction runs from north to south; inside it returns from south to north.

Iron, nickel and cobalt are familiar strongly magnetic materials at ordinary temperatures. Many steels are strongly attracted, but some stainless steels are not. Aluminum, copper, pure gold and ordinary plastic do not stick to a stationary classroom magnet. Their weak magnetic responses are different from the strong attraction in this test. Alloys matter: a U.S. copper-nickel five-cent coin does not behave like pure nickel. A sticking test gives evidence about a material, but cannot identify its composition by itself.

Electric **current** produces a magnetic field. A current-carrying coil forms an **electromagnet**, often strengthened by a soft iron core. Changing the current changes the field. Opening the circuit stops the coil current, although the core may keep some magnetism. More turns can strengthen a coil when current and geometry are comparable; adding wire also changes resistance. Use only the teacher-approved current-limited kit described in the activity.

Electromagnets help cranes lift and release steel. Release must still be tested: residual magnetism or tangled objects can keep a load attached. Permanent magnets can also be used in devices with mechanical release mechanisms. Speakers use a changing coil current interacting with a magnetic field to move a cone.

Earth’s main field is sustained by motion of electrically conducting fluid in its liquid outer **core**. The inner core is solid. A **compass** aligns with the horizontal component of the local magnetic field, which usually differs from true geographic north. Near the northern magnetic region, the field enters Earth, so that region behaves like a bar magnet’s south pole. Magnetic and geographic poles are not the same locations.

cards.target: An electromagnet's superpower: it can be switched off
essentialFacts: Electricity and magnetism are two faces of one thing; a current in a wire makes a magnetic field (Ørsted, 1820).
Coil a wire around an iron core and run current through it to make an electromagnet.
More turns can strengthen the field at comparable current and geometry. Stopping current removes the coil-produced field, but a core can retain magnetism.
Cranes and many devices use controllable magnetic fields; some also use permanent magnets.
cards.aiExample: A permanent magnet is a light with no switch: always on. An electromagnet is the same light with a wall switch: the current is the switch, the coil is the bulb, and more current is a brighter bulb.
cards.mapping: The switch controls coil current and its field. A real core may retain magnetism, so the light analogy has limits. More turns only predict a stronger field when other conditions are comparable.

history.title: Field Test

questions.question: You bring the north poles of two magnets together. What happens?
options: They pull together strongly
Nothing — poles only matter for compasses
They push each other apart
One pole flips to become a south pole

questions.question: You cut a bar magnet exactly in half. What do you have?
options: One north-only magnet and one south-only magnet
Two pieces of ordinary metal with no magnetism
One magnet twice as strong and one dead piece
Two complete magnets, each with a north and a south pole
questions.correctAnswer: Two complete magnets, each with a north and a south pole

questions.question: Why does a magnet stick strongly to a carbon-steel door panel but not to an aluminum can in an ordinary stationary test?
options: Carbon steel is strongly magnetic; aluminum is not strongly attracted in this test
The can is too smooth for the magnet to grip
Aluminum blocks magnetic fields entirely
The door is colder than the can
questions.correctAnswer: Carbon steel is strongly magnetic; aluminum is not strongly attracted in this test

questions.question: In the simple bar-magnet comparison, which polarity describes Earth’s northern magnetic region where field lines enter Earth?
options: A magnetic north pole, matching the name
South-like polarity; a compass follows the local field rather than exact geographic north
The North Star's gravity
Nothing — compasses use gravity, not magnetism
questions.correctAnswer: South-like polarity; a compass follows the local field rather than exact geographic north

questions.question: What is the single biggest practical advantage of an electromagnet over a permanent magnet?
options: It never loses strength over time
It works without any metal nearby
It attracts every material equally
It can be switched off and on
questions.correctAnswer: It can be switched off and on

questions.question: Explain why a controllable electromagnet is useful for lifting and releasing steel. Could a permanent-magnet design also release a load?
questions.expectedAnswer: Switching off coil current reduces the electromagnet’s field, helping release steel. Residual magnetism and tangled objects can affect release, so it must be tested. A permanent magnet can also release a load with a mechanical stripper or other release mechanism.

questions.question: The reading says a magnetic field acts 'through empty space with no touching.' Describe one experiment you could do to show this is true.
questions.expectedAnswer: Bring a classroom magnet toward a steel paperclip while keeping a visible air gap. The clip can move before contact. This demonstrates magnetic force at a distance through air; it does not by itself test a vacuum.

reflections.text: What surprised you most: the cut-magnet result, or that north is really south? Explain.
List three things in your home that would stop working without electromagnets.

history.title: Magnet Questions

data.question: Can magnets really erase a phone or a credit card? 💳
data.answer: Old magnetic-stripe cards, yes — a strong magnet can scramble the stripe. Modern phones and chip cards are far more resistant, though very strong magnets can still confuse a phone's compass sensor temporarily.

data.question: Why do magnets get weaker over time?
data.answer: Heat, hard impacts, and stray opposing fields gradually knock the tiny aligned regions inside out of formation. Drop a magnet enough times and you genuinely weaken it.

data.question: Has Earth's magnetic field ever flipped? 🌍
data.answer: Many times — the rock record shows north and south have swapped repeatedly over millions of years. The last full reversal was roughly 780,000 years ago. It takes thousands of years to complete, not a day.

data.question: Does dividing a bar magnet separate its north and south poles?
data.answer: No. In this thought experiment, each piece is a smaller magnet with north and south poles. This result does not require physically cutting a magnet.

data.question: Are humans magnetic?
data.answer: Most body tissue has a very weak diamagnetic response: it is weakly repelled by a strong, nonuniform magnetic field. That is very different from iron sticking strongly to a classroom magnet.

data.question: Why do speakers need magnets? 🔊
data.answer: A coil carrying a changing current sits in a magnet's field. The changing current makes the coil push and pull against that field, vibrating a cone and creating sound. Your music is literally magnetism moving air.

data.title: A Sorter That Lets Go
data.instructions: Design a small tabletop sorter that picks steel paperclips from a clean mixed sample and releases them into a tray. Use a teacher-approved classroom electromagnet kit or demonstrate a permanent magnet with a mechanical release. Test pickup and release separately.
data.fitReason: The reading names the electromagnet's single biggest advantage: it can be switched off. A sorter that must pick up AND let go forces students to use that fact rather than recite it.

brief.context: Model recycling with five carbon-steel paperclips, clean aluminum-foil pieces, plastic counters and paper pieces on a tray. Available materials are a teacher-approved current-limited low-voltage electromagnet kit, a classroom magnet, cardboard, string and tape. Use the kit’s supplied switch and instructions; do not connect loose wire directly across a battery.
brief.audience: The custodian and the school's green team
brief.drivingQuestion: How can a tabletop device pick out the steel paperclips and then release them into a separate tray?
brief.seedDirection: Two problems hide in one: grabbing only steel, and letting go on command. Decide which magnet type solves the second problem before you design the first.
lockedLessonFacts: Iron, nickel, cobalt and many steels are strongly attracted. Aluminum, copper, pure gold and ordinary plastic do not stick in this stationary classroom test; alloys vary.
A magnetic field acts through empty space; the force is strongest closest to the poles.
A current-carrying coil creates a field. Compare turns only at comparable current and geometry; adding wire also changes resistance.
Switching off current reduces an electromagnet’s field, but residual magnetism and tangled objects can affect release.
Opposite poles attract and like poles repel.
openQuestions: How many paperclips can the approved kit lift during its permitted operating time?
How close must the magnet be before a paperclip moves?
Can changing the pickup distance improve results while keeping the approved electrical settings fixed?
Will aluminum cans ever come along by accident, and why or why not?
stakeholders: The custodian who sorts by hand now
The green team that tracks recycling
The recycling company that rejects mixed loads
criteria: Picks up at least four of five steel paperclips from the sample
Records any foil, plastic or paper carried along accidentally
Releases the lifted paperclips into the tray on command; records any failures
The design sheet explains each choice with a lesson fact
constraints: Use only the teacher-approved current-limited low-voltage kit and its instructions, or a non-electrical mechanical-release model
Keep the kit’s settings fixed and follow its operating-time limit; disconnect and tell the teacher if anything warms unexpectedly
Use clean small test objects over a tray; do not lift full cans or use loose-wire battery circuits
Must be testable in one class period
brief.deliverable: A labeled design sketch, a built prototype or a detailed build plan, a test table (item, picked up yes or no, released yes or no), and a short explanation that uses at least four glossary words.

parallelExample.context: A scrap yard needed to separate steel from a mountain of mixed metal.
parallelExample.move: An electromagnet can lift strongly attracted iron and steel from a mixture. Turning off its current helps release the load. Other objects may be carried along mechanically, and residual magnetism can affect release; engineers test these limitations.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: It is your problem at full scale: the material rule does the sorting, and the off switch does the releasing.

supports.frameStarter: Our sorter uses ____ because ____. It lets go by ____.
frameChoices: An electromagnet on a string that we switch off over the steel bin
A permanent magnet with a cardboard sleeve that lets paperclips be pushed off
A ramp with a magnet underneath that pulls steel cans off course
A rotating drum with an electromagnet inside one section
coachPrompts: Why should the foil stay behind, and how could it still get carried along accidentally?
